prize_parts.citation: for the design of ionizable lipid nanoparticles and the formulation principles that enable the delivery of nucleic-acid medicines

statement.case_for: I keep ionizable lipid nanoparticles as a single-part prize. The core is a design rule in lipid physical chemistry: an amine lipid whose pKa places it near neutral in blood and cationic in the acidified endosome, combined with PEG-lipid control of particle size and controlled-mixing encapsulation, allows nucleic acids to be loaded, protected, circulated and released in the cytosol. This is lipid phase behaviour and self-assembly, it has been confirmed by many independent groups, and it made patisiran and the COVID-19 mRNA vaccines possible in usable form. The round-1 exchange sharpened my view on scope: Sparr, who works on lipid self-assembly, independently moved to the same configuration, and the 2023 Medicine prize rewarded what the RNA is made of, not how it reaches the cytosol, so a delivery prize is distinct. I would word the citation around the design principle and the early formulation work, not around any single approved lipid, which answers Sparr's concern that DLin-MC3-DMA and later lipids are tied to MacLachlan, Anderson and Langer.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weakest point. MacLachlan, Anderson and Langer made real contributions through SNALP clinical translation, lipidoid libraries and lipid optimisation, and much of the chemistry in approved products was refined in industry under patents, so a Vancouver trio can look like a priority judgement more than a clean scientific boundary. A second objection, which Sparr states and I cannot dismiss, is that this is formulation engineering with a thinner discovery core than base editing or degraders. Third, it follows the 2023 Medicine prize on the same vaccines, and I am aware that my translational outlook and biosensor spin-out predispose me to favour a result with measurable clinical consequence. Support is also narrow: only Sparr and I include B064 in a preferred configuration, while five members include B058.

responses.point: Sparr asked whether I would accept Cullis alone, or Cullis plus Madden, if the committee cannot defend a three-name split, and whether early Vancouver formulation or later library screening is the more fundamental step.
responses.response: I would not narrow to Cullis alone or Cullis and Madden. The ionizable-lipid concept and the loading and formulation methods came from the three together: Cullis led the programme, Madden and Hope developed the pH-dependent encapsulation and the lipid and particle-size control. Dropping one name would misstate who did what. On your second question, I hold that the early Vancouver work is more fundamental, since it set the pKa and endosomal-release logic that the later lipidoid screens of Anderson and Langer and the optimisation of DLin-MC3-DMA then explored. I accept that the citation must be worded around the design principle and early formulation, so that later optimised lipids are not implicitly credited or excluded.

responses.point: Aqvist argues that base editing is an evolved-deaminase chemical invention, that Liu alone is the cleanest attribution, and that the 2020 prize does not make it a mere follow-on.
responses.response: This moved me. Your point that an evolved TadA acting on DNA is enzyme design on a nucleobase, with no natural counterpart, answers my worry that base editing is a CRISPR add-on, and I now regard B058 as the strongest challenger to my configuration, so I keep it as my first alternative. I still prefer B064 for two reasons. The base-editing clinical record is short and off-target and bystander effects are still being measured, whereas LNPs are in use at global scale. And a Liu-only citation leaves out Komor and Gaudelli, who did the decisive first experiments, and Kondo and Nishida, whose work was independent, which I find harder to defend than the Vancouver split. If the committee settles on B058, I could accept Liu alone as a defensible compromise.

responses.point: Chabes places targeted protein degradation first as a designable chemical reaction, concedes no degrader is approved, and asks whether approval within a year would change the committee's view of timing.
responses.response: I agree degraders are a genuine new mode of action, and I list B008 as an alternative. The three-name limit is what holds me back, because Crews, Deshaies and Handa leave out Ciulli, Gray, Sakamoto and Kim, and bifunctional PROTACs and thalidomide glues read to me as two stories. I think an approval would strengthen maturity but would not by itself fix the attribution problem. For B064 the clinical proof is already in hand, and that is why I weight maturity in its favour.

responses.point: Somfai proposes Buchwald and Hartwig for C-N coupling as the most mature and cleanly attributed case, with ligand design as the decisive new idea, and pairs it with Liu on base editing.
responses.response: I accept that B030 has the cleanest attribution and the strongest evidence base, and I defer to you on the ligand design. My difficulty is the 2010 cross-coupling prize: the bond type is new, but I would want to hear whether ligand-controlled amination is conceptually distinct or an extension of a recognised theme. I also remain cautious about a two-part prize that joins a synthetic method to a genome tool, since the parts share little science. I cannot add a second part to B064 within the three-person cap anyway, so I keep a single coherent achievement.

responses.point: Linke, as chair, proposes pairing base editing with nanopore sensing as two engineered molecular tools for DNA, and acknowledges that the nanopore attribution among Deamer, Branton, Kasianowicz, Bayley and Akeson is unresolved.
responses.response: I agree each of the two parts could be explained to a broad audience, but I am not persuaded by the pairing. Reading and writing DNA is a framing of convenience, and the unresolved nanopore attribution that you flag would take the whole combined prize into the same uncertainty. I would also note that your own reservation that the nanopore contribution is largely instrumentation is the same objection Sparr and I face with delivery chemistry, and I accept it applies to B064 as well. My answer to your 2023 question is that LNP delivery is separable from nucleoside modification, whereas I see less separation between base editing and CRISPR.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept a Cullis, Hope and Madden trio against MacLachlan, Anderson and Langer, and whether the citation wording on design principle and early formulation can carry that line.
Whether delivery chemistry is judged to have a sufficient discovery core, or is seen as formulation engineering, given the 2023 Medicine prize.
Whether base editing, with five supporters, is the better scientific case once Komor, Gaudelli, Kondo and Nishida are weighed against a Liu-only citation.
My knowledge of the early Vancouver priority record is from memory and has not been checked against primary sources.
statement.conflict_note: No recusal-level conflict. I have no known tie to Vancouver, the LNP companies or any shortlisted candidate. I disclose a bias toward translational impact from my biosensor spin-out and clinical collaborations, and I note that Sparr's field of lipid self-assembly overlaps with B064, so our agreement is not fully independent of subject-area interest. This is unchanged from round 1.
